name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I farm Costa's Field with my dad, who's semi-retired and still thinks he's in charge. It's 45 hectares: about 120 outdoor pigs, field vegetables, and a veg box scheme that goes out to 300 households on Thursdays. My mornings are pigs and planning, afternoons are picking and packing. I run the whole box scheme off an AI assistant now, the orders, the route, the emails when the courgettes fail. My partner Ana is a part-time nurse, and our boys, Leo and Tomas, are ten and seven.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mud and margins. The pigs churn the field to soup every winter and the supermarket price for pork hasn't moved in years. The box scheme is what keeps us afloat. I'm also trialling a little solar weeding robot from the growers' co-op, which I adore and my dad calls the Roomba.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, that would be a letdown for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. I'd still tell people at the growers' co-op it saves me a day a week on the box scheme admin. I'd probably post a short thread about the weeding robot being slower than promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping the robots would get good enough to take the back-breaking jobs and make small farms like ours easier to run. If it all stalls, we're stuck with the same margins and the same mud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for the box scheme and push it a bit further, maybe to plan crop rotations and predict demand. I'd keep the weeder on trial and give honest feedback to the co-op. And I'd keep saving our usual 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of disappointment. Like a promised holiday that turned into a long weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI actually do for you on a Thursday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI builds the delivery route around which customers are home, and it writes the 'sorry, no leeks this week' email in a way that doesn't sound like I'm crying. Last Thursday it saved me about two hours. My dad still prints the order list out on paper and checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be pleased if it stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, definitely. He'd say 'told you so' about the Roomba every day for a month. Ana would be pleased too, honestly, because she thinks I spend too long fiddling with gadgets.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle. It still saves me a day a week on the box scheme admin.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed. I was hoping robots would take the back-breaking jobs and make small farms easier to run, but we'd be stuck with the same margins and mud.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for the box scheme and stretches it to crop rotation planning and demand forecasting. Keeps the weeding robot on trial, gives feedback to the co-op and keeps saving 150 a month.
S0.quote: The AI builds the delivery route around which customers are home, and it writes the 'sorry, no leeks this week' email in a way that doesn't sound like I'm crying.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the rare farmer who would be let down if AI stalled. He sees robots as relief from hard physical work on a small farm. His father's scepticism comes up repeatedly and seems to be part of the family humour.

steps.text: Keep the solar weeding robot on trial and give the growers' co-op honest feedback
Stretch the box scheme's AI assistant to plan crop rotations and predict demand
Keep saving the usual 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's more or less what I'm planning for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms have to get in early and share the kit, or the big ones will hoover up the benefit. I'd say that at the growers' co-op and online. And I'd argue for public grants so the machines aren't just for the rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could do well out of this. A couple of shared robots for weeding and pig feeding, and suddenly I've got time to grow the box scheme to 500 households. The risk is that the supermarkets get the same robots and squeeze prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put about 6,000, nearly all our savings, into a co-op share of two weeding robots and a feeding system for the pigs. I'd use AI to work out which veg earn the most per hour. And I'd try to sign up 100 more box customers before the supermarkets work out what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, with a small knot about spending the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Nearly all your savings is a big bet with a mortgage. What does Ana think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana would make me write it all down, the costs, the worst case, what we'd do if the robots broke. We'd agree to keep one month's money back no matter what. My partner Ana is the brake and I'm the accelerator, and that's why the farm still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our seasonal pickers, mostly. We hire four people every summer, and two of them have come back for eight years. I'd want to keep them on packing and deliveries, but I can't promise that.

S1.say: Small farms have to get in early and share the kit, or the big ones will take all the benefit. There should be public grants so the machines aren't just for the rich.
S1.think: I could do well out of this, with shared robots giving me time to grow the box scheme to 500 households. The risk is that supermarkets get the same robots and squeeze prices.
S1.do: Puts about 6,000 of savings into a co-op share of two weeding robots and a pig feeding system, keeping one month's money back. Uses AI to rank crops by earnings per hour and tries to sign up 100 more box customers.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, with a knot about spending savings.
S1.quote: My partner Ana is the brake and I'm the accelerator, and that's why the farm still exists.
S1.fieldNote: Marco sees steady disruption as an opportunity and would move his savings into shared robots fast. His partner acts as a check on risk. He worries more about his seasonal pickers than about himself.

steps.text: Put about 6,000, nearly all the savings, into a co-op robot share, keeping one month back
Bring two shared weeding robots and a pig feeding system onto the farm
Use AI to work out which vegetables earn the most per hour

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office jobs go first and the muddy ones last. Huh. That flips it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers aren't the first in line this time, the desk jobs are, and we should be making noise for the people who lose them in 2028. At the growers' co-op I'd say we've got about three years before the robots, so this is the moment to buy shared kit before the big farms get it. Online I'd keep banging on about an AI dividend, a payment to everyone from the money the machines make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own work is mostly hands-on, so I've got till 2031 before a robot can pick a courgette as well as me. The box scheme admin I already hand to the AI, so 2028 makes that bit even easier. What scares me is my 300 households. Half my veg box customers work in offices in town, and if they lose their pay in 2028, the first thing they cancel is a 22-a-week veg box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is stop the plan to grow to 500 boxes and hold onto our cash instead. I'd add a cheaper 'basics' box at about 12 a week, so people who lose work can drop down instead of quitting. I'd still put about 3,000 into the co-op's shared weeding robots, half what I'd planned, and keep two months of money back. I'd start a Saturday market stall in town, so I'm not relying on one kind of customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but wide awake. It's the feeling of a storm coming when you've still got time to get the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your box list are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a woman on the Thursday round who does claims at an insurance firm, she's ordered every week for six years and leaves a note when the eggs are good. That's exactly the kind of job the AI takes in 2028. I'd rather give her a box on credit than lose her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got three years before your own work is touched. Doesn't that feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, yes, about my own hands. But a farmer with steady hands and no customers is just a man with a nice garden. The three years are for getting the customers through, not me.

S2.say: Farmers aren't first in line this time, the desk jobs are, and we should make noise for the people who lose them in 2028. Small farms have about three years to buy shared kit before the big farms get the robots.
S2.think: My own work is mostly hands-on, so I've got until 2031, and the box scheme admin only gets easier. What scares me is my 300 households, because half work in offices in town and a 22-a-week veg box is the first thing they'd cancel.
S2.do: Halts the plan to grow to 500 boxes, adds a cheaper basics box at about 12 a week, and starts a Saturday market stall. Still puts about 3,000 into the co-op's shared weeding robots while keeping two months of money back.
S2.feel: Anxious but wide awake, like a storm coming while there's still time to get the hay in.
S2.quote: Half my veg box customers work in offices in town, and if they lose their pay in 2028, the first thing they cancel is a 22-a-week veg box.
S2.fieldNote: Marco worked out the order of events faster than most: thinking AI hits his customers' office jobs three years before robots touch his own. His plans are all about keeping his buyers, not protecting his own labour. He still invests in robots, just more carefully than in the steady scenario.

steps.text: Drop the 500-box growth plan and add a 12-a-week basics box
Start a Saturday market stall in town for a second set of customers
Put about 3,000 into the co-op's shared weeding robots, keeping two months back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and then three more. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version small farms can win, if we buy the machines together and early. I'd tell the co-op we need a plan for 2034 written by next spring. And I'd push for cheap public loans for shared robots, so we own them instead of renting them from a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. By 2031 the AI does all the planning, by 2034 the robots do the digging, and I'd be 51 and running a farm that people visit as much as buy from. My worry is still the customers, but five years gives the town time to find its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd put about 4,000 into shared robots through the co-op and keep two months of savings. I'd let the AI plan the crop rotations and the box routes completely. With Ana I'd start planning school visits and a pick-your-own patch for 2028, so there's a part of the farm that's about people, not just veg.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Uneasy only when I think about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad make of school visits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble and then be the star of it. My dad's got sixty years of stories about pigs escaping onto the main road, and kids would love him. A robot can weed a bed, but it can't make a ten-year-old laugh about a runaway sow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said uneasy about the town. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the basics box going and give the co-op's surplus to the food bank instead of composting it. It's small. But if we're the ones doing well out of robots, we'd better share some of it.

S3.say: This is the version small farms can win, if we buy the machines together and early. We need cheap public loans for shared robots, so we own them instead of renting them from a big company.
S3.think: I think this is good for me: the AI plans by 2031, the robots dig by 2034, and I'd be running a farm people visit as much as buy from. Five years also gives the town time to find its feet.
S3.do: Puts about 4,000 into shared robots through the co-op while keeping two months of savings, and hands crop rotations and box routes fully to the AI. Plans school visits and a pick-your-own patch with Ana for 2028.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit excited, uneasy only when he thinks about the town.
S3.quote: A robot can weed a bed, but it can't make a ten-year-old laugh about a runaway sow.
S3.fieldNote: With eight years before robots, Marco sees opportunity rather than threat. His plan turns the farm toward visitors, with his father's stories as part of the offer. He's conscious that doing well out of robots brings a duty to share.

steps.text: Put about 4,000 into shared co-op robots, keeping two months of savings
Hand crop rotations and box routes completely to the AI
Plan school visits and a pick-your-own patch with Ana for 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years to robots. Leo would be 23.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. At the co-op I'd say let's teach this ourselves rather than wait for the dealers. I'd keep pushing the AI dividend idea, because the end point is the same even if it comes slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd love this. I'd use the AI to plan everything from day one and have shared robots on the farm well before 2039. The only thing I'd miss is coming in filthy, if robots do all the dirty work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short agricultural robotics course at the college, about 600, in the first year so I could teach other growers later. I'd save 50 a month for each of the boys' training. I'd add a robot pig feeder through the co-op by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pretty excited. Like a long run-up to something I've wanted for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd miss coming in filthy. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's how I know I've worked. I like coming in filthy, and Ana makes me strip off in the porch. If robots do the dirty work, I'll have to find something else to be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Leo and Tomas to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whatever they love, honestly, but I'd want them to understand machines. Leo already takes apart the weeder when I'm not looking. If my son ends up fixing robots for the whole valley, I'd be thrilled.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. The co-op should teach this ourselves rather than wait for the dealers, and the AI dividend still matters because the end point is the same.
S4.think: I'd love this, with AI planning everything from day one and shared robots on the farm well before 2039. The only thing I'd miss is coming in filthy once robots do the dirty work.
S4.do: Takes a short agricultural robotics course at the college for about 600 in year one so he can teach other growers. Saves 50 a month for each son's training and adds a co-op robot pig feeder by year three.
S4.feel: Calm and quite excited, like a long run-up to something he's wanted for years.
S4.quote: I like coming in filthy, and Ana makes me strip off in the porch. If robots do the dirty work, I'll have to find something else to be proud of.
S4.fieldNote: With the long timeline Marco is purely positive about his own future, and the only loss he names is the pride of physical work. He wants to become a teacher of the new machines, not just a user. His eldest son already shows the same curiosity.

steps.text: Take a 600 agricultural robotics course at the college to teach other growers
Add a shared robot pig feeder through the co-op by year three
Save 50 a month for each of Leo's and Tomas's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of the robots, but because my customers in the offices would lose their jobs three years before a robot could even pick a courgette, and before anyone sorted out how to share the money. What would help is a proper AI dividend paid to everyone, and cheap co-op loans so small farms can own their machines instead of renting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who's going to buy the food. Everyone asks if farmers survive. But a farm with no customers is just a garden.

headlineQuote: A farm with no customers is just a garden.
portrait: Marco Costa, 43, runs Costa's Field, a 45-hectare pig and vegetable farm with a 300-household veg box scheme, alongside his semi-retired father. He uses AI every day and is trialling a weeding robot, and he'd be disappointed if AI stalled. He'd put savings into shared robots under steady change. Fast AGI makes him anxious not for his own hands-on work, which has until 2031, but because his office-worker customers would lose their pay in 2028, so he'd add a cheaper box and a market stall. With five or ten years he's calm, planning school visits, robotics teaching and his sons' training, and always argues for shared ownership of the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his office-worker customers would lose their incomes three years before robots reach farm work, and before anyone worked out how to share the gains.
whatWouldHelp: An AI dividend paid to everyone, and cheap co-op loans so small farms can own their machines rather than rent them.
